name: Tactile Depth
tagline: A dark-first premium app shell where real recipe photography glows against layered near-black surfaces.
thesis: Paul's Cookbook should feel like a funded, high-craft mobile product: compact controls, cinematic food imagery, precise metadata, and a floating side drawer that turns utility into something tactile. The design refuses the generic recipe-site card wall by treating every recipe as a polished object and every control as part of a browsing cockpit.

typography.ui: Inter if present, system UI fallback
typography.numeric: JetBrains Mono if present, SFMono/Consolas fallback
typography.scale: 16px base with a 12.5% large-text preference; card titles never below 16px, metadata never below 13px, micro labels never below 11px

moves: Dark-first layered surfaces with one committed copper/amber accent and restrained optical glow.
A sticky morphing control dock combines search, live count, sort direction, and category grouping without stealing browse space.
Recipe cards behave like tactile objects: rounded, lifted, image-led, with no floating black metadata chips from the incumbent design.
Prep time and price use inline tabular numerals with quieter units and explicit partial/unavailable price states.
The side menu is a floating panel with elevated depth, focus trapping, body scroll lock, tactile filter chips, category jumps, more links, and preferences.
Light mode is warm porcelain and copper with its own depth system rather than a naive dark inversion.
Empty state, focus rings, reduced motion, long Romanian titles, and 320px no-overflow behavior are designed as first-class seams.
tradeoffs: The hero is intentionally atmospheric but compact; it uses real catalogue photos without adding editorial claims or recommendations.
The control dock stacks on narrow screens to preserve 44px touch targets and readable text instead of compressing controls into tiny icons.
Cards can vary in height because full recipe titles are never clipped; this preserves content integrity over masonry-perfect rows.
